"Did you call?" Afreen asked, closing the hostel door.

"Yes. The college counselling centre. Thursday at four," Tanuja said.

"Proud of you. What will you say?"

"That's the thing. I'll forget it all when I sit down."

"Then write it. Give me your pen."

"Okay. For about a month I've been waking at five and can't get back to sleep. I don't want to eat. Nothing feels fun, even my favourite show."

"Add that you've been skipping the group project calls."

"Right. Should I say it's silly?"

"No. You wouldn't call a broken wrist silly. Just hand them the page."

Tanuja folded the paper into her diary and, for the first time in weeks, let out a long breath.

qa.q: When is Tanuja's session at the counselling centre?
Why did Tanuja ask whether she should say it was silly?
qa.a: Tanuja feared her problems might seem small or a sign of weakness, so she wanted to be reassured about asking.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja bring to the session, and why?
qa.a: Tanuja could bring a list of questions along with the summary, because it helps her use the time well when nerves make her forget.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel about helping Tanuja write the page?
qa.a: Afreen likely feels glad to help and hopeful, having pushed gently by comparing it to a broken wrist so Tanuja would treat it as normal care.

grounding: A student books a counselling session and writes a short symptom summary, treating professional help as a normal step.

subtype: Approach: book an appointment with a counsellor or psychiatrist [Action]
passage:
I'm Kunal. In March I went to the campus doctor, Dr Vijay, about headaches and not sleeping. After a few questions, the doctor asked how my mood had been, and I surprised myself by telling the truth: low for about two months, nothing feels worth doing, stopped going to practice. Dr Vijay said it was worth talking to someone trained for this, and gave me the college counselling centre's number and a helpline in case things felt worse before the appointment.
I walked around campus for twenty minutes before calling. Part of me thought counselling was for people with 'real' problems. Then I thought: I came to a doctor for headaches without feeling weak. This is the same.
I booked Thursday at 4. That night I wrote half a page to take with me: sleeping badly for two months, not hungry, stopped football, feeling far away from friends, worse on Sundays.
On Thursday my hands were cold. But I had the page, and I read from it.

qa.q: When did Kunal book the counselling session?
How did Kunal feel before calling the counselling centre?
qa.a: Hesitant and a bit ashamed, worried counselling was only for 'real' problems, then steadier after comparing it to seeing a doctor for headaches.

qa.q: Why is Kunal's half-page summary useful?
qa.a: It lets Kunal share the main points even with cold hands and nerves, so nothing important is left unsaid.

qa.q: How might Dr Vijay see Kunal's honest answer?
qa.a: As an important step, since asking about mood uncovered more than headaches and led to the right kind of help.

grounding: Shows a student booking a counselling session on a doctor's suggestion and writing a short summary to share, treating it as a normal step.

Warden's note, Block B, 14 November. Shalini.
Deepika, second year, came to my office this evening and asked, very quietly, how students book the college counsellor. She said she had been 'not herself' for weeks: sleeping in the afternoons, skipping the mess, crying after calls home without knowing why. She added quickly, 'It's probably nothing. Other people have bigger problems.'
I told her booking a counsellor is as ordinary as booking a doctor, and that I'd do it with her if she liked. We rang the centre together from my office phone. The first slot was Monday at 11. I also gave her the student helpline card and told her she could knock on my door any evening before then.
Before she left, she asked for paper and wrote a few lines to take to the session: when it started, what has changed, what she hopes for. She folded it into her ID card holder.
I will check in with her on Saturday and again after Monday.

qa.q: When is Deepika's first counselling slot?
What does 'Other people have bigger problems' suggest about how Deepika feels?
qa.a: She feels unsure she deserves help, maybe a little ashamed to ask, even though she is struggling.

qa.q: What else could support Deepika before Monday?
qa.a: The warden's Saturday check-in, and a friend she trusts knowing about the appointment.

qa.q: How does the evening look to Shalini, the warden who wrote the note?
qa.a: Shalini sees a student taking a brave step and makes it easy, booking together and staying available until the session.

grounding: Shows a student booking the college counsellor with a warden's help and writing a short summary to take, treated as an ordinary step.
